correctness.rationale: A complete finite proof enumerates every integer partition into >=3 arm lengths up to nine edges; for each shape, all binary arm words modulo precisely the equal-length arm-permutation automorphisms are considered. A second direct vertex-pair path enumerator checks every profile. A closed multiset orbit formula cross-checks completeness; exact outputs include all 25 nine-edge shapes, 5788 colorings, 5786 topology-scoped profiles, precisely the two named doubletons, and none smaller. The delivered code was replayed successfully. No infinite extrapolation is claimed.

originality.rationale: The novelty assessed is the sharp known-topology binary spider first-failure cutoff and exact exceptional fiber identification, not the general path-Parikh polynomial or the existence of colored-tree nonreconstructibility. Bartha 2021 already aggregates all binary signed-tree confusability data for ten vertices, but does not state or logically entail which fixed spider shape has the two explicit doubleton fibers. Targeted research-index and web searches found no equivalent statement. Priority remains qualified by unindexed records and possible unreleased data behind the 2021 aggregate census.
residual_risks: Bartha 2021 all-tree census may have unpublished underlying instance-level output containing these pairs; publicly inspected Table 3.5 does not expose it.
Unindexed prior exact parameter surveys or unpublished theses may have obtained the same first-spider classification.
The result is finite up to nine edges and does not predict larger-spider behavior.

value.rationale: Known-topology binary path-Parikh reconstruction of a singly branching tree is a natural first graph extension of substring-composition reconstruction. The sharp smallest edge count, unique topology, exact two ambiguous fibers and complement symmetry give a complete obstruction classification for the smallest nontrivial alphabet in the smallest branching graph family, useful as finite recovery limits and test instances. This is distinct from a generic table total and does not require a new all-order theorem.
